source.title: ExpertLens: Activation steering features are highly interpretable
source.authors: Masha Fedzechkina; Eleonora Gualdoni; Sinead Williamson; Katherine Metcalf; Skyler Seto; Barry-John Theobald

page_placements.theme: Apparent polysemanticity often reflects one coherent shared or related feature

record.file_problem: The paper text is substantially complete, but its abstract begins mid-word/sentence and is garbled at the start.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses individual neurons identified by the finding-experts method as its analysis units and explicitly assumes that concept representations align with the neuron basis. It measures expert-set stability and human alignment, but does not test the listed claims about the share of neuron poles with one main job, the cited explanation-evaluation procedures, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The study reports results about neuron-based expert representations, including their stability, semantic alignment, and effects of activating them. Those results do not measure the job-count shares or explanation-prediction scores named by V1–V7. The activation-generation results are deliberately induced by activating experts. Embedding comparisons and results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study treats finding-experts neurons as analysis units and states it assumes concepts align with the neuron basis. It reports the tool's stability, human alignment and steering effects. It never estimates the share of neurons with one main job, scores explanations by simulation, studies InceptionV1, or builds attribution graphs. So none of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that ExpertLens concept representations are stable across models and datasets, and that they align with human similarity judgments near inter-human levels. They add that this alignment exceeds embeddings, reconstructs domain structure, and makes ExpertLens a lightweight interpretability tool. They note the neuron-basis assumption and the single-word-concept scope as limitations.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies the finding-experts method, ranking units by average precision on positive and negative example sets, then analyzes expert-set overlap and its relation to human concept judgments. It does not use the claim's Qwen3 pole audit or the explanation-on-held-out-activations procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Expert-set overlap varies with the AP threshold τ; the pilot reports small sensitivity to dataset generation model and positive/negative set sizes, with higher τ reducing overlap. Human alignment also varies with model size and training checkpoint.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors say expert neurons are polysemantic along human-interpretable lines: 'cat' experts overlap with 'dog' but not 'car'. Neurons responding to unrelated concepts are not predictive, so they don't enter expert sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Pythia models, neurons predictive of a concept are shared mainly with semantically related concepts, not unrelated ones.

fits_no_version.finding: Gemma-2b and Gemma-2b-it expert overlap correlates with MEN human similarity, comparably to similarly sized Pythia models. The instruction-tuned model is slightly higher, but not significantly (App. F, Fig. 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert-set alignment with human similarity holds in Gemma-2b and is not significantly changed by instruction tuning.

record.problems: The study examines single-word everyday concepts and says this task may be too simple to distinguish models. It assumes concept representations align with the canonical neuron basis and studies neurons individually. Several results are summarized from figures without exact numerical values; the reported activation-generation result has an apparent inconsistency between the stated fifty-concept list and the 60-concept result.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted to meet the row limit. Figure-only expert-count and layer-location plots are not transcribed because they do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no shares of neurons with one, two or unknown jobs.
Pythia 70m–12b, GPT-2 and Gemma-2b are studied, but no per-neuron job shares; no MoE or trillion-scale models.
No InceptionV1, cat-and-car neuron, pose or recursive generalization analysis.
No test of architecture, regularization or tooling effects on the interpretable-neuron share.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
No held-out prediction test of explanations fit to activating examples.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from uses_without_test to assumes, because the paper explicitly assumes concepts align with the canonical neuron basis. Steering rows (R8, R9) are induced effects and are not claim evidence. No original source of the claim is involved.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or estimate the percentages of poles with one main job, two related jobs, or unknown jobs.
Studies Pythia models up to 12b and Gemma-2b, but does not estimate the claimed shares of neuron poles across models, dense/MoE architectures, or trillion-parameter models.
Does not study InceptionV1 or the cat-and-car example, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not test the proposed architecture/tool explanation or the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or compare their reconstruction error with a trained replacement model.
Does not test whether explanations fit to activating examples predict where neurons fire on held-out activations.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: The Limitations section says outright that the analysis assumes concepts align with the neuron basis, and it never tests the share of interpretable neurons. So 'assumes' fits the text. 'uses_without_test' would also be defensible, but the given label is not wrong.

tranche.reason: The study uses the finding-experts method as a tool and reports its own method's stability and human alignment. It does not test whether neurons have one main job.

source_check.notes: The Figure 1 caption swaps the inter- and intra-concept labels. Within-concept overlap is about 0.8 at tau=0.5, and overlap between random different concepts is about 0 (GPT-2 pilot). The cat/dog/car polysemanticity remark is an unquantified author statement in Limitations, and 'car' is not in the domain concept list. The cat-dog overlap appears for Pythia-12b in Section 4 and Fig. 4. Cited row R2 is the GPT-2 pilot, not Pythia. R6 and R7 measure domain-level overlap, not the share of neurons with one main job.
